How ethnocentrism shows up in language, food, and customs
Enculturation as the reason ethnocentrism is a natural habit

claims.claim: Ethnocentrism is the tendency to interpret or evaluate other cultures in terms of one's own — the working definition used in this lesson.

William Graham Sumner introduced the term 'ethnocentrism' in the social sciences, describing it in his 1906 book Folkways as the view of things in which one's own group is the center of everything and all others are scaled and rated with reference to it.

OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology defines ethnocentrism as the notion that one's own culture is so superior that no other culture is worth consideration; ethnocentric people often imagine the world would be a better place if the beliefs, values, and practices of their own culture were spread to or imposed on everyone else.

Enculturation — the process of learning and acquiring one's own particular culture, often intensified in childhood — happens to every human being, and it is natural to value the knowledge gained through one's own enculturation because it is how people learn to live.

Ethnocentrism is a widespread habit that grows out of enculturation, and it becomes harmful when a group's conviction of its own superiority leads it to dismiss, harm, exploit, or dominate other groups; historically, European ethnocentrism was used to justify subjugation of peoples in Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and the Americas.

Ethnocentric lenses have corrupted scientific observation: even early anthropologists mischaracterized non-Western peoples — as without religion or as having a 'prelogical mentality' — because they measured them by Western European standards, and ethnocentric observers do not bother to learn about or consider other ways of doing things.

Pride in one's own culture or country is not the same as ethnocentrism: the defining move of ethnocentrism is rating other cultures by one's own standards (Sumner: all others 'scaled and rated' with reference to one's own group), so affection for one's own group alone does not constitute the bias.

positions: OpenStax presents ethnocentrism as ubiquitous — a consequence of enculturation that every human being experiences because everyone is raised inside some culture.

Britannica suggests the tendency 'has been, perhaps, more prevalent in modern nations than among preliterate tribes,' tying prevalence to how much exposure a group has to culturally different neighbors.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that ethnocentrism is a common default that grows out of enculturation, and it avoids comparative claims about which societies are more or less ethnocentric. It also keeps the honest framing that a default is not a destiny: OpenStax's own section is titled 'Overcoming Ethnocentrism,' so the lesson presents noticing and setting the bias aside as a learnable skill rather than an impossibility.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does ethnocentrism require hostility or contempt toward outsiders?
positions: Sumner's original account includes contempt for outsiders: each group 'looks with contempt on outsiders' and thinks its own folkways the only right ones.
OpenStax's glossary centers on superiority and the wish to impose one's own ways, while noting ethnocentric people do not value other perspectives.
Wikipedia notes the term 'does not necessarily involve a negative view of the others' race' — the judgment-by-own-standards core can operate without racial hostility.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the judgment-by-own-standards core as the definitional move and treats superiority, dismissal, and imposition as common accompaniments rather than required ingredients. This keeps the definition precise without equating ethnocentrism with racism.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced machine-generated boilerplate with source-verified content throughout.

Added enculturation as the mechanism explaining why ethnocentrism is natural, per OpenStax section 1.3.
Kept the historical styles (primitivism, orientalism) as one-line supporting context only, since the detailed history belongs to other topics.
All examples (market stall, dinner-table roommate, mountain-town research notes, flag-flying Nina, journalist Mara) are original to this lesson.

Supports: the egocentric/ethnocentric parallel; ethnocentrism as the conviction that one's own ways of understanding the world and doing things are best and no other ways are worth consideration; enculturation as the process of acquiring one's particular culture, undergone by all humans; the naturalness of valuing the knowledge gained through one's own enculturation; the harm of ethnocentrism when it justifies subjugation and violence; primitivism and orientalism as historical styles of ethnocentrism (Said attribution). Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Folkways: A Study of the Sociological Importance of Usages, Manners, Customs, Mores, and Morals (William Graham Sumner, 1906)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary text read via Gutenberg plain-text copy (ebook 24253, pg24253.txt). Section 1.15 'Ethnocentrism': 'Ethnocentrism is the technical name for this view of things in which one's own group is the center of everything, and all others are scaled and rated with reference to it... Each group thinks its own folkways the only right ones.' Supports the Sumner coinage and the group-centered definition, and the claim that pride/vanity in one's own group is separable from the rating of others. One short attributed quotation used.
